hints: Think about the leaf having two opposite problems - it needs to let gases in and out, but every open pore also lets water escape. When would the benefit outweigh the cost?
Link daytime to photosynthesis. Which raw material for the Calvin cycle can only enter through open stomata, and why is light relevant?
Link night-time to no photosynthesis. If carbon dioxide is not needed in the dark, what is the advantage of closing to water balance?
walkthrough:
Daytime Need - Gas Exchange for Photosynthesis**
In the light, mesophyll cells photosynthesise rapidly and need a supply of carbon dioxide for the light-independent stage / Calvin cycle. The only route in is by diffusion through open stomata, so opening in the day maximises photosynthesis.

Night-time Need - Conserve Water**
In the dark there is no light for photosynthesis, so there is no benefit in taking in carbon dioxide. Open stomata would only allow water vapour to diffuse out in transpiration, risking wilting. Closing at night therefore reduces water loss when uptake of carbon dioxide is not useful.
Final answer: Open in day / light to take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis / Calvin cycle. Close in night / dark to reduce water loss by transpiration.

hints: Start with energy. Opening is not passive - think about what is actively pumped out of the guard cell cytoplasm using ATP to set up the rest of the sequence.
After positive ions leave, consider how the electrical charge inside the guard cell changes and what type of membrane channel this will open next.
Once solute ions accumulate inside, think about the effect on water potential and which way water will then move by osmosis.
Link water entry to turgor and volume change of the two guard cells surrounding each pore.
Remember that potassium is not the only solute - think about which negative ion also enters to maintain balance.
Finish with structure to function - recall why the unevenly thickened guard cell walls make turgid cells curve apart rather than just swell.
walkthrough:
Set Up An Electrical Gradient With Proton Pumps**
Light triggers proton pumps in the guard cell plasma membrane. They use ATP to actively transport $H^+$ / protons out of the cytoplasm. The inside becomes more negative relative to the outside.

Solute Ions Flood In**
The negative interior opens voltage-gated $K^+$ channel proteins, so $K^+$ moves in down its electrochemical gradient by facilitated diffusion. $Cl^-$ ions also move in. This greatly increases solute concentration inside.

Osmosis Makes Cells Turgid**
More solutes lowers / makes more negative the water potential of the guard cell. Water therefore moves in from surrounding epidermal cells by osmosis down a water potential gradient. The guard cells swell, increase in volume and become turgid with high turgor pressure.

Unequal Walls Turn Swelling Into Bending**
Each guard cell has a thick, inelastic inner wall lining the pore and a thin, elastic outer wall. When turgid, the outer wall stretches more, so the pair bend / curve outward. The pore between them widens - this is the open stoma seen rising to about 85-90% in Fig. 2.1 in the first 7 hours.

Final answer: $H^+$ pumped out of guard cell using ATP / energy, leaving cell interior more negative; $K^+$ channels open and $K^+$ enters by facilitated diffusion, $Cl^-$ also enters; solute / water potential of cell decreases, water enters by osmosis; cells become turgid and swell; thicker inner wall and thinner outer wall causes cells to bend / curve apart, pore opens.

hints: Compare Fig. 2.1 with Fig. 2.2. In normal light-dark cycles peaks reach about 80-90% open, but in continuous darkness from 14 hours what happens to peak height and regularity?
Ask yourself what it means if a roughly 24-hour cycle of opening and closing still continues with no light cue at all - what internal mechanism must be keeping time?
walkthrough:
Light As Environment Keeps The Rhythm Full and Normal**
In Fig. 2.1 with 14 h light and 10 h dark, opening peaks regularly at about 80-90%. In Fig. 2.2 in continuous darkness the peaks are lower, falling to about 60-65% and becoming less regular. So the environmental cue of light is needed to entrain the rhythm and achieve full opening.

Genes Provide An Internal Clock**
Even without any light after 14 hours, a roughly daily cycle of opening and closing still continues for days in Fig. 2.2. This cannot be a direct response to light, so it must be controlled internally by genes - an endogenous circadian rhythm.

Final answer: Environment / light needed to keep rhythm normal / to achieve same high peak % opening as in Fig. 2.1; peaks fall to about 60% in Fig. 2.2. Genes have a role as regular rhythm / cycle continues in continuous darkness, showing endogenous / circadian control.
